title: Backtracking
subtitle: FAANG & Hard OA Preparation Guide
author: Mayank | IIIT Kottayam
overview:
Backtracking is systematic trial-and-error: you build a candidate solution incrementally, one choice at a time, and the moment a partial candidate can no longer lead to a valid complete solution, you **undo the last choice** ("backtrack") and try the next option. It is exhaustive search with pruning — it explores the full state-space tree implicitly, but cuts off branches early using constraints, which is what keeps it from being pure brute force.

Backtracking is the natural stepping stone into Dynamic Programming. Almost every DP problem starts life as a backtracking/recursion solution: you first write the recursive "try every choice" version, then notice overlapping subproblems and add memoization, turning exponential backtracking into polynomial DP. Mastering backtracking first is what makes the DP transition intuitive rather than magical.
coreConcept:
Every backtracking problem follows the same skeleton:

1. **Choose** — pick one option from the choices available at this state.
2. **Explore** — recurse into the new state with that choice made.
3. **Un-choose (backtrack)** — undo the choice so the next sibling option starts from a clean state.

Think of it as a depth-first traversal of a decision tree, where each node is a partial solution and each edge is a choice. The recursion goes deep until it hits a **base case** (solution complete) or a **dead end** (constraint violated), then unwinds.

coreConceptBoxes.body: The recursion tree IS the search space. Backtracking doesn't build the whole tree in memory — it walks it depth-first, one root-to-leaf path at a time, reusing the same variables (arrays, lists, visited sets) by mutating and un-mutating them. This in-place mutate/un-mutate discipline is what separates efficient backtracking code from wasteful copy-heavy code.

triggerWords: "generate all...", "find all possible...", "return all valid..." → exhaustive enumeration
"place N queens/objects such that..." → constraint satisfaction backtracking
"partition into...", "split the string/array such that each part satisfies..." → partition backtracking
"does there exist a path such that..." in a grid/graph → path backtracking (DFS with undo)
structureSignals: Answer is a *set of all valid configurations*, not a single optimal number (that's usually DP/Greedy instead)
Small input size in constraints (n ≤ 12–20 for permutation-like problems, board ≤ 9×9) — a strong hint that exponential search is intended
Choices at each step are clearly enumerable (pick next character, next number, next cell)
A validity/pruning check can be applied *before* recursing deeper, not just at the end

variationsSummary.keyIdea: Choose k out of n, order doesn't matter
Split at every valid cut point

variations.name: Subsets / Powersets
variations.coreIdea: For each element, you have exactly two choices: include it in the current subset, or don't. Branching on this binary choice for all n elements naturally generates all 2^n subsets.

items: The recursion tree has depth n and each node branches into 2 — total leaves = 2^n.
Every partial path from root to any node (not just leaves) is itself a valid subset — that's why subsets are usually added to the answer at *every* recursive call, not just at the base case.

When duplicates exist in the input, sort first, then skip a duplicate value if its previous identical sibling at the same recursion depth was NOT chosen (this avoids generating the same subset twice).
**Two-choice template**: at index i, either add `nums[i]` then recurse on i+1, or skip it and recurse on i+1 — cleanest way to think about include/exclude.

**Iterative "for-loop" template**: alternative style where at each recursive call you loop `for j = start..n-1`, add `nums[j]`, recurse with `start = j+1`, then remove — avoids explicit include/exclude branches and is easier to adapt to combinations/permutations.
**Duplicate skip**: `if (j > start && nums[j] == nums[j-1]) continue;` after sorting — the single most important trick for "II" variants across this entire pattern.

solved.title: Subsets
solved.statement: Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible subsets (the power set).

boxes.body: No duplicates to worry about. Straightforward include/exclude on every index.
Every prefix of the recursion path is a valid answer, so we push `path` into the result at the start of every call, then try extending it with each remaining element in turn.

bruteForce.approach: Generate all 2^n bitmasks from 0 to 2^n-1, and for each bitmask include `nums[i]` if bit i is set.
bruteForce.space: O(n) auxiliary (excluding output) — same asymptotic cost as backtracking but less natural to extend to duplicates/pruning

optimal.approach: Backtracking with the for-loop template; record the path at every node.

complexity.timeNote: 2^n subsets, each costing O(n) to copy into the result

solved.title: Subsets II
solved.statement: Given an array that *may* contain duplicates, return all possible unique subsets.

boxes.body: Same tree as Subsets, but without pruning, duplicate values at the same recursion depth generate the same subset multiple times — e.g. `[1,2,2]` would produce `[1,2]` twice from the two different 2's.

Sort the array first so identical values become adjacent. At any recursion level, if we are about to pick `nums[j]` and `nums[j] == nums[j-1]` while `j > start` (meaning the previous identical element at this exact level was already tried and fully explored, not chosen), skip it — this prunes the duplicate branch without needing a hash set.

bruteForce.approach: Same bitmask enumeration as Subsets, then dump all 2^n subsets into a `HashSet<List<Integer>>` to deduplicate.
bruteForce.space: O(2^n * n) for the intermediate set — wasteful since we build duplicates only to throw them away

optimal.approach: Sort, then skip duplicate siblings at the same recursion level.

complexity.timeNote: worst case (no duplicates), fewer in practice with duplicates

solved.title: Letter Case Permutation
solved.statement: Given a string with letters and digits, return all strings you can create by transforming each letter to lowercase or uppercase (digits stay fixed).

boxes.body: Digits contribute no branching (only 1 choice); letters contribute exactly 2 choices (lower/upper). This is the include/exclude template applied to a character transformation instead of an array element.
Walk the string index by index. At a digit, just copy it forward with no branch. At a letter, branch into two recursive calls — one with the lowercase version, one with the uppercase version.

bruteForce.approach: Count k = number of letters, generate all 2^k bitmasks, and for each bitmask build the corresponding string.

optimal.approach: In-place character mutation; both branches overwrite the same index so no explicit undo is needed.

complexity.timeNote: k = number of letters, n = string length

variations.name: Permutations
variations.coreIdea: Unlike subsets, *order matters* — every element must appear exactly once, but in every possible arrangement. At each recursive step you pick any *unused* element (not just ones after the current index) to place next.

items: A `boolean[] used` array (or swapping in-place) tracks which elements are already placed in the current path.
Total leaves = n!, since at depth i there are (n-i) remaining choices.

For "Permutations II" (duplicates in input), the same duplicate-skip trick from Subsets applies, but now it's checked against `used[j-1]` rather than the loop start — this distinction trips up most people the first time.
**Used-array template**: cleanest and most extensible — track a boolean per index rather than physically removing/adding elements.
**In-place swap template**: swap `nums[start]` with `nums[j]`, recurse on `start+1`, swap back — avoids extra space but is trickier to adapt for duplicate-skipping.

**Duplicate skip for permutations**: after sorting, `if (nums[j] == nums[j-1] && !used[j-1]) continue;` — skipping when the previous identical value is *not currently used* ensures duplicates are only placed in a fixed relative order.

templates.label: Permutations skeleton

solved.title: Permutations
solved.statement: Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible permutations.

boxes.body: No duplicates, so no skip-logic needed — pure "pick any unused element next" recursion.
At every recursion depth, loop over all indices; if not yet used, place it, recurse one level deeper, then unplace it. Base case is when `path` has length n.

bruteForce.approach: Generate permutations via Heap's algorithm or repeated swapping without a used-array, effectively the same asymptotic cost. A truly naive approach: generate all n^n sequences and filter for those using every element exactly once. Backtracking with a used-array is already the practical "brute force" here since n! is the true output size.
bruteForce.time: O(n^n) for the naive filtering approach

complexity.timeNote: n! permutations, each costing O(n) to copy into the result
complexity.spaceNote: used array and recursion depth, excluding output

solved.title: Permutations II
solved.statement: Given an array that may contain duplicates, return all unique permutations.

boxes.body: Without the duplicate-skip check, swapping identical values into the same position produces identical permutations multiple times — e.g. `[1,1,2]` would produce `[1,1,2]` twice.

Sort first. When deciding which value goes into the current slot, among a run of equal values only allow the *first not-yet-used* one to be tried — enforced by `if (nums[j]==nums[j-1] && !used[j-1]) continue;`. This forces equal values to be used in their original left-to-right order across siblings, eliminating duplicate branches.

bruteForce.approach: Generate all permutations as in LC 46 (ignoring duplicates), then insert each into a `HashSet<List<Integer>>` to dedupe.
bruteForce.space: O(n! * n) for the intermediate set of all permutations before dedup — very wasteful for inputs with many duplicates

optimal.approach: Sort + used-array with the `!used[j-1]` duplicate skip.

complexity.timeNote: worst case (all distinct), far fewer valid branches when duplicates exist
complexity.spaceNote: used array and recursion depth, excluding output

variations.name: Combinations
variations.coreIdea: Choose a subset of a fixed size k (or satisfying a sum/count constraint) from n elements, where order does *not* matter. This is Subsets restricted with an extra stopping/pruning condition (size == k, or running sum reaches target).

items: Same "for loop from start" template as Subsets, but you only record the path when it satisfies the target condition, not at every node.
Combination Sum allows *reusing* the same element (recurse with `j`, not `j+1`) — a subtle but critical variant.
Generate Parentheses is a "constructive" combinations problem: instead of picking from an array, you pick from a fixed alphabet {(, )} at each step, constrained by counts.
**Reuse-allowed**: pass `j` (not `j+1`) as the next start index when the same element can be picked multiple times (Combination Sum).
**Early pruning by sort**: sort input first; if `nums[j] > remainingTarget`, break the loop immediately (everything after is even bigger) — huge speedup for Combination Sum family.

**Constraint-tracked construction**: for Generate Parentheses, track `open` and `close` counts directly instead of validating the whole string at the end — prune the instant a constraint would be violated.

problems.title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number

solved.title: Combination Sum
solved.statement: Given distinct candidate numbers and a target, find all unique combinations where chosen numbers sum to target; the same number may be reused unlimited times.

boxes.body: Because repetition is allowed, this is not exactly Subsets — the same index can be revisited. The recursion depth is bounded not by n but by `target / min(candidates)`.

Sort candidates first. At each step, either use the current candidate again (staying at index `j`) or move to the next candidate (`j+1`) once you decide not to use it further. Prune the moment `candidates[j] > remaining`, since the array is sorted and everything after is larger too.

bruteForce.approach: Try every possible multiset of candidates up to `target/min` length via nested loops without pruning, checking sums after the fact.
bruteForce.time: exponential without early cutoff, effectively O(2^target) in the worst case — pruning is what makes this practical

optimal.approach: Sorted candidates + reuse-allowed recursion + break on overflow.

complexity.timeNote: worst case bound by branching over reuse decisions, pruned heavily in practice by the sorted-break

solved.title: Generate Parentheses
solved.statement: Given n pairs of parentheses, generate all combinations of well-formed parentheses strings.

boxes.body: A string of parentheses is well-formed iff at every prefix, `open count` >= `close count`, and by the end both counts equal n. This means we can validate *incrementally* instead of checking the whole string at the end.

At each recursive call, we have two possible characters to add: '(' (only if `openCount < n`) or ')' (only if `closeCount < openCount`, so it never exceeds the open count). This constraint-tracked construction prunes every invalid branch immediately rather than generating and filtering.

bruteForce.approach: Generate all 2^(2n) binary strings of length 2n (each position either '(' or ')'), then filter for well-formed ones by scanning each string.
bruteForce.space: O(2^(2n) * n) before filtering — massively wasteful compared to constrained construction

optimal.approach: Track open/close counts and only branch into legal characters.

complexity.timeNote: the n-th Catalan number bounds the output size, and each valid string costs O(n) to build

variations.name: N-Queens / Sudoku
variations.coreIdea: Place objects on a board one at a time (row by row, or cell by cell) subject to hard constraints (no two queens attack each other; no repeated digit in row/column/box). The moment a placement violates a constraint, prune immediately instead of completing the placement first.

items: N-Queens places exactly one queen per row, so the recursion depth is bounded by n (number of rows), with the loop trying each column in that row.

Constraint checks (column used? diagonal used? anti-diagonal used?) should be O(1) using boolean arrays/sets indexed by `col`, `row+col`, and `row-col` — never re-scan the whole board on every placement.
Sudoku instead searches cell by cell (or picks the most-constrained empty cell first) and tries digits 1–9, validating row/column/3x3-box constraints.
**Diagonal encoding**: for an n×n board, `row+col` uniquely identifies a "\\" diagonal and `row-col+n-1` uniquely identifies a "/" diagonal — track both in boolean arrays for O(1) conflict checks.

**Fail fast, return boolean**: for Sudoku, make the recursive function return `true` the instant a full valid solution is found, short-circuiting all pending loops instead of continuing to explore already-solved boards.

**Most-constrained-cell heuristic**: solving the emptiest-choice cell first (fewest valid candidate digits) drastically prunes the Sudoku search tree in practice, though the basic version (first empty cell) is sufficient for interviews.

templates.label: Board placement skeleton

solved.title: N-Queens
solved.statement: Place n queens on an n×n chessboard such that no two queens attack each other. Return all distinct board configurations.

boxes.body: Since exactly one queen must go in each row, we can reduce the search to: for each row, try each column, and check that the column, and both diagonals, are free.

Maintain three boolean sets: `cols`, `diag1` (indexed by `row+col`), `diag2` (indexed by `row-col+n-1`). Before placing a queen at `(row, col)`, check all three are free in O(1); after backtracking, clear all three.

bruteForce.approach: Try all C(n^2, n) ways to place n queens anywhere on the board, then validate each full placement for attacks.
bruteForce.time: astronomically large and impractical even for n=8 — this is why row-by-row placement with incremental pruning is essential, not optional

optimal.approach: Row-by-row placement with O(1) column/diagonal conflict checks.

complexity.timeNote: worst case, roughly — each row has fewer valid choices than the last due to pruning

solved.title: Sudoku Solver
solved.statement: Fill a partially filled 9×9 Sudoku grid so every row, column, and 3×3 sub-box contains digits 1–9 exactly once.

boxes.body: Unlike N-Queens, the search isn't cleanly row-by-row — we scan for the next empty cell and try digits 1–9 there, validating against the row, column, and box simultaneously.

Because we only need *one* valid solution (not all), the recursive function should return a boolean and short-circuit (return `true` immediately) the instant a full solution is found — this avoids continuing to explore an already-solved board.

bruteForce.approach: Try every combination of digit fills for all empty cells independently, validating the whole board only at the very end.
bruteForce.time: O(9^81) in the absolute worst case with zero pruning — completely infeasible; incremental per-cell validation is mandatory

optimal.approach: First-empty-cell search with per-placement validation and boolean short-circuit.

complexity.timeNote: exponential in theory for m empty cells, but heavily pruned in practice by per-placement validation — runs fast on real puzzles
complexity.spaceNote: in-place on the board, plus recursion depth up to 81

variations.name: Word Search / Path in Grid
variations.coreIdea: Explore a 2D grid via DFS, trying to build a path (word, or maximal path) cell by cell. Mark the current cell as visited before recursing into neighbors, and **unmark it** on the way back up — this is what allows the same cell to be reused on a different path attempt.

items: The "visited" marking is exactly the choose/un-choose backtracking discipline applied to grid cells instead of array elements.
A common trick to avoid a separate `visited[][]` array: temporarily overwrite the cell's value with a sentinel (e.g. `'#'`) then restore it after exploring — saves memory and an extra parameter.
Branching factor is up to 4 (or 8 with diagonals) per cell, and the recursion depth equals the target path length L, giving worst-case O(4^L) paths explored per starting cell.
**In-place visited marking**: overwrite `board[r][c]` with a sentinel character instead of allocating a boolean grid — restore the original character when backtracking.
**Early character mismatch pruning**: check `board[r][c] == word.charAt(idx)` *before* recursing, not after — avoids wasted recursive calls entirely.
**Try all starting cells implicitly**: loop over every `(r,c)` in the grid as a potential starting point for the first character, since the path can start anywhere.

templates.label: Grid DFS with undo

solved.title: Word Search
solved.statement: Given an m×n grid of characters and a word, return true if the word exists in the grid, formed by adjacent (horizontally or vertically) cells without reusing the same cell twice.

boxes.body: The word must be traced as a connected path, and no cell can be revisited within the same path — this is exactly the visited-marking DFS pattern.

Try every cell as a possible start of the word's first character. From a matching cell, mark it visited and DFS into all 4 neighbors looking for the next character; if any neighbor path completes the word, propagate `true` up; otherwise restore the cell and report failure to the caller.

bruteForce.approach: From every starting cell, try all possible paths of length `word.length()` via unrestricted DFS without early character-matching, then compare the final built string to `word`.
bruteForce.space: same asymptotic bound as the optimal version, but wasteful in constant factor since mismatches aren't pruned until the whole path is built

optimal.approach: DFS with in-place sentinel marking and early mismatch pruning.

complexity.timeNote: L = word length; mn possible starting cells, each spawning a search bounded by 4^L
complexity.spaceNote: recursion depth (board is modified in-place, no extra grid needed)

variations.name: Partition into Subsets
variations.coreIdea: Split a sequence (string or array) into contiguous pieces such that every piece individually satisfies some property (palindrome, equal sum, valid word, etc.). At each recursive step, try every possible "next cut point" and recurse on the remainder.

items: The choice at each step is *where to cut next*, not which element to pick — subtly different framing from Subsets/Combinations but same choose/explore/un-choose skeleton.
Precomputing a palindrome-check table (or memoizing substring validity) turns an O(n) per-check cost into O(1), which matters a lot since this check happens inside the branching loop.
Partitioning into k equal-sum subsets requires tracking k running bucket sums simultaneously and pruning symmetric/duplicate bucket assignments (skip empty buckets that already failed).
**Precompute validity table**: for palindrome partitioning, build `isPalin[i][j]` via DP in O(n^2) before backtracking, so every substring check inside the recursion is O(1).
**Cut-point loop**: `for (end = start+1; end <= n; end++)` — try every possible length for the next piece starting at `start`.
**Bucket-sum pruning for k-partition**: sort descending and skip identical bucket-sum states (`if (j > 0 && buckets[j] == buckets[j-1]) continue;`) to avoid re-exploring symmetric failed assignments.

problems.title: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets

solved.title: Palindrome Partitioning
solved.statement: Given a string, partition it such that every substring in the partition is a palindrome. Return all possible palindrome partitionings.

boxes.body: At every position `start`, we try every possible `end` for the next piece, and only recurse if `s[start..end)` is a palindrome — this is a direct application of the cut-point template.

Naively checking if a substring is a palindrome takes O(n) each time, and we do this check O(n) times per recursion level across O(n) levels — precomputing an `isPalin[i][j]` table with simple DP (`isPalin[i][j] = s[i]==s[j] && isPalin[i+1][j-1]`) makes each check O(1), which matters because the recursion branches heavily.

bruteForce.approach: Try all 2^(n-1) ways to place cut points between characters (each gap either cut or not), then validate every resulting piece is a palindrome and filter.
bruteForce.space: checking palindromes on the fly without precomputation multiplies cost by O(n) per check

optimal.approach: Precompute the palindrome table, then backtrack over cut points with O(1) validity checks.

complexity.timeNote: worst case — up to 2^(n-1) valid partitions, each costing O(n) to materialize; palindrome table build is O(n^2), dominated by the partitioning cost
complexity.spaceNote: palindrome table plus O(n) recursion depth

commonMistakes: **Forgetting to un-choose**: not removing the last element from `path` (or not restoring a mutated cell/array) after the recursive call returns — this silently corrupts every subsequent sibling branch.

**Copying the reference instead of a snapshot**: adding `path` directly to `result` instead of `new ArrayList<>(path)` — since `path` keeps mutating, every stored reference ends up pointing to the same final (usually empty) list.

**Wrong duplicate-skip condition**: using `used[j-1]` logic in a for-loop-based template (Subsets/Combinations) or using `j > start` logic in a used-array template (Permutations) — these two skip conditions are *not* interchangeable; mixing them either misses valid results or lets duplicates through.
**Not sorting before duplicate-skipping**: the "skip if equal to previous" trick only works if identical values are adjacent, which requires sorting first.

**Redundant validity re-scans**: re-checking the entire board/row/column on every single placement instead of maintaining incremental state (boolean sets for columns/diagonals, or a precomputed palindrome table) — this turns an efficient pruning approach into an accidentally quadratic (or worse) one.

**Off-by-one in reuse vs no-reuse**: passing `j` instead of `j+1` (or vice versa) as the next start index — this is the single line that separates "elements can repeat" (Combination Sum) from "elements are used once" (Subsets/Combinations).
**Missing base case entirely**: forgetting to handle the case where the input is empty, or where `k=0` in a combinations problem — always trace through the smallest possible input by hand.
interviewTips: Always state the **state-space tree** out loud first: what is a node (a partial candidate), what is a choice (an edge), what is the base case (a leaf)? Interviewers want to see this framing before code.
Estimate time complexity using the *constraints*: if n ≤ 12 and answer wants "all permutations," O(n!) is expected and fine — don't over-engineer trying to find a polynomial solution.

Mention the connection to DP explicitly when relevant: "this is the exponential backtracking version; if we only needed a count/optimal value instead of all solutions, we could memoize overlapping `(start, remaining)` states and turn this into DP." This shows depth of understanding.

Always mutate and restore state in place rather than passing copies of arrays/lists down the recursion — interviewers notice when candidates default to expensive copying instead of the leaner choose/un-choose discipline.
For grid/graph based backtracking, explicitly ask about grid size and whether the same cell can be revisited — this changes whether you need a visited marker at all.
Practice explaining the pruning condition as "why does trying this branch further guarantee failure" — that's the crux interviewers probe for beyond just working code.
